title: Ant on a Prism: Which Corner Comes First? | AMC 10-Style Level 4

scenes.visual: Prism (brief: figure). Line 1: an ant dot hops C->B->C->F along edges, one hop per ~0.6 s (dot to dot, no off-edge paths). Line 2: E glows green with a flag, A glows red; '?' between them. Line 3: Vantee title card.
lines: An ant wanders a prism, one random edge a second. Finish line or trap: which corner comes first?
I'm Vantee, and today we're racing an ant to the finish line!

scenes.visual: Question text left, prism right. Line 2: bottom triangle ABC then top DEF draw on. Line 3: edges AD, BE, CF highlight. Line 4: ant at C; its 3 edges pulse. Line 5: E green, A red. Line 6: 5 value chips 1/3, 4/11, 5/11, 6/11, 7/11 (NO letters A-E: they clash with vertex names).
lines: A triangular prism has a bottom triangle, A B C, and a top triangle, D E F.
Edges A D, B E and C F join each bottom corner to the one above it.
An ant starts at corner C. Each second, it crawls along one of the three edges at its corner.
All three edges are equally likely. What's the chance it reaches E before it ever reaches A?
Here are the five choices. Take a good look.

scenes.visual: Line 1: E tag 'finish' (green), A tag 'trap' (red). Line 2: a sample walk C->F->D->A ends at A (red X), the ant stops. Line 3: goal card 'P(E before A), start C'.
lines: Let's sort out the facts. E is the finish line, and A is the trap.
The walk ends at whichever one the ant reaches first. Sooner or later, it's sure to reach one.
So we want the chance that E comes first, starting from C.

scenes.visual: Pause card with countdown ring; prism with green E / red A visible.
lines: Now it's your turn. Pause the video and give it a go. I'll wait!

scenes.chapter: Solution 1: a chance for every corner
scenes.visual: Prism left, equation rows right. Line 2: chips c, b, d, f at C, B, D, F; '1' at E, '0' at A. Line 3: from B, three arrows each labelled 1/3. Line 4: rule card 'chance = average of the 3 neighbours'. Lines 5-8: highlight the vertex and its 3 neighbours, write its row.
lines: Welcome back! Here's the strategy: give every corner its own chance of winning.
From C, call it c. Do the same for B, D and F. E counts as one, and A as zero.
Each neighbor is next with chance one third. So a corner's chance is the average of theirs.
B touches A, C and E. So b equals zero plus c plus one, all over three.
D touches A, E and F. So d equals zero plus one plus f, all over three.
C touches A, B and F. So c equals zero plus b plus f, all over three.
F touches C, D and E. So f equals c plus d plus one, all over three.

scenes.visual: Rows build one per step (brief: solve). The c-row and f-row results get boxed; line 4 adds them; line 7 answer badge 4/11, chip 4/11 lights green, chime at END of line 7.
lines: Start with the rule at C. Multiply by three: three c equals b plus f.
Swap in b, then multiply by three again. Nine c equals one plus c plus three f.
So eight c equals one plus three f.
The same steps at F, using d, give eight f equals four plus three c.
Now a neat trick: add them. Eight c plus eight f equals five plus three c plus three f.
Take away three c and three f: five c plus five f equals five. So c plus f equals one!
Then f is one minus c. So eight c equals one plus three minus three c, and eleven c equals four.
So c is four over eleven. That's our answer!

scenes.visual: Line 1: 'c + f = 1' card from solve. Line 2: front face ABED tinted, A and E circled, diagonal A-E dashed. Line 3: skewer through face centre and CF midpoint; prism spins 180 deg about it (brief: spin), labels ride along. Line 4: pairs A<->E, B<->D, C<->F with swap arrows. Line 5: two mini-cards: 'start F, race to E' = 'start C, race to A'. Line 6: rows f = 1 - c, d = 1 - b.
lines: Here's a faster way. That c plus f equals one was no accident.
Look at the front face, A B E D. A and E are opposite corners.
Push a skewer through the middle of that face, and spin the prism half a turn.
A and E swap places. So do B and D, and so do C and F. It's the same prism!
So an ant at F racing to E is just like an ant at C racing to A.
From C, A comes first with chance one minus c. So f equals one minus c, and d equals one minus b.

scenes.visual: Rows (brief: spin-solve). Line 4 answer badge 4/11 again (chime at end). Line 5: C's edges: one to red A, none to green E. Line 6: card 'Look for a spin that swaps win and loss'.
lines: Now plug f equals one minus c into our rule from before: eight c equals one plus three f.
So eight c equals four minus three c. Eleven c equals four. Four over eleven again!
When would you pick this way? Whenever a spin swaps the win and the loss. Look for it first.

scenes.visual: Value chips; each wrong one turns red with its working (brief: traps). Prism small at the side with the solved chances 0, 5/11, 4/11, 6/11, 1, 7/11 at A..F.
lines: Now let's look at the wrong answers.
One third is what you'd get if you guessed b and f are one half each. They aren't.
Five over eleven is b, the chance from B. Right work, wrong corner.
Six over eleven is the chance from D, the letter d. Also the wrong starting corner.
Seven over eleven is one minus c, the chance that A comes FIRST. That's the race backwards.

scenes.chapter: Your turn: a new finish line
scenes.visual: Same prism. Ant at C. Line 2: E loses its green; F turns green 'finish'; A stays red 'trap'. Line 3: question card 'P(F before A), start C'.
lines: Ready for a challenge? Same prism, and the ant starts at C again.
Now F is the finish line, and A is still the trap. What's the chance F comes first?

scenes.visual: Pause card, countdown; prism with green F, red A, ant at C.
lines: Pause the video, and go for it!

scenes.visual: Line 1: face ACFD tinted, A and F circled; skewer + 180 deg spin about its centre and the midpoint of BE (brief). Line 2: pairs A<->F, C<->D, B<->E; row e = 1 - b. Lines 3-6: rows (brief). Line 6 badge 5/11, chime at end.
lines: Let's check. A and F are opposite corners of the face A C F D. Skewer it and spin.
A swaps with F, C with D, and B with E. So e equals one minus b.
At C: c equals zero plus b plus one, all over three.
At B: three b equals c plus one minus b, so four b equals c plus one.
From the C rule, b equals three c minus one. Swap it in: twelve c minus four equals c plus one.
So eleven c equals five, and c is five over eleven. If you got it, amazing work!

scenes.visual: Summary card, two rows with a small prism: '1. chance = average of the neighbours' / '2. a spin swaps win and loss -> paired chances add to 1'.
lines: Give every corner a chance. Each one is the average of its neighbors' chances.
Then look for a spin that swaps the win and the loss. Paired chances add up to one.
I'm Vantee. Happy exploring, and see you next time!
